pathways.name: Papez circuit and hippocampal trisynaptic circuit
pathways.function: Limbic circuitry for episodic memory and emotional processing, linking the hippocampal formation, hypothalamus, thalamus and cingulate cortex

steps.neurotransmitter: glutamate (not directly stated in sources; unsourced)

evidence.quote: The hippocampus then connects to the mammillary bodies via the fornix (FX).
The mammillary bodies project to the ventral thalamus via the mammillothalamic tract (MTT).
The mammillothalamic is a projection bundle that arises from the mammillary bodies, projects dorsally, and cranially, toward the thalamus.

courseVia: anterior limb of the internal capsule

evidence.quote: the ATR fibers connect the thalamic midline and anterior nuclear groups with the frontal lobe by traversing through the anterior limbs of bilateral internal capsules
The ventral thalamus links back into the prefrontal cortex and anterior cingulate gyrus via the thalamo-cingulate projections (TC) to complete the Papez circuit

The CB is the longest limbic pathway of the Papez circuit generating a large loop connecting the prefrontal projections of the cingulate gyrus to the hippocampus in the parahippocampal gyrus of the temporal lobe

steps.cellBodies: Entorhinal cortex (layer II, weakly layer V)
steps.neurotransmitter: glutamate (not directly stated for this step; unsourced)

evidence.quote: The outer two thirds are targeted mainly by layer II (and more weakly by layer V) of the entorhinal cortex via the perforant path
It contains the axons of the granule cells (i.e., the mossy fibers) and is the site at which they form the en passant synapses on the proximal dendrites of CA3 pyramids

decussation.where: some Schaffer collateral/associational fibres cross via the hippocampal commissure to the contralateral hippocampus

evidence.quote: The collaterals of the giant CA3 pyramids which target the CA1 region have been named Schaffer collaterals after the first neuroanatomist to describe them
Canonical pathways encompass the classic trisynaptic loop from the entorhinal cortex (EC) to dentate gyrus (DG), CA3, CA1, and subiculum (SUB).

lesions.site: Mammillary bodies, anterior/mediodorsal thalamic nuclei, mammillothalamic tract (thiamine deficiency)
lesions.deficit: Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome: severe anterograde amnesia and executive dysfunction

evidence.quote: In Korsakoff syndrome, injury involving the mammillary bodies, anterior and mediodorsal thalamic nuclei, mammillothalamic pathways, and connected hippocampal and frontal networks contributes to severe impairment of episodic memory and executive function.

lesions.site: Bilateral medial temporal lobe (hippocampus, amygdala, surrounding cortex) surgical excision
lesions.deficit: Dense, global anterograde amnesia (patient H.M. / Henry Molaison)

evidence.quote: The original account by Scoville and Milner (1957) described that in the 10 patients studied, including H.M., the severe anterograde memory impairments occurred only after bilateral MTL excisions that included much of the amygdala, hippocampus, and surrounding cortex.

conflicts.issue: Role of the subiculum in the trisynaptic/hippocampal circuit

positions.claim: Subiculum is the classic fourth output stage terminating the trisynaptic pathway
positions.quote: the subiculum has been considered the “fourth leg” and output region of the trisynaptic pathway

positions.claim: Subiculum is better characterised as an integration hub receiving and redistributing hippocampal, thalamic and cortical afferents rather than a simple output relay
positions.quote: recent evidence highlights the subiculum as a site of integration, receiving and redistributing outputs from the hippocampus, anterior thalamus, retrosplenial cortex, and entorhinal cortex

unsourced: The perforant path and mossy fibre / Schaffer collateral synapses use glutamate as their principal neurotransmitter (physiological convention; not explicitly stated with a citation in the opened sources for every step).
Some fornix and hippocampal commissural fibres decussate, allowing bilateral hippocampal communication (general anatomical convention; not explicitly quoted from an opened source for this batch).

pathways.name: Amygdala fear circuit
pathways.function: Rapid detection and behavioural/autonomic response to threat; fear conditioning and anxiety

steps.cellBodies: Sensory thalamic relay nuclei (e.g. medial geniculate body for audition, other sensory thalamic nuclei for other modalities)
steps.neurotransmitter: glutamate (not explicitly stated in opened sources for this exact step)

evidence.quote: consists of direct anatomical projections from visual thalamic nuclei to the amygdala (a key structure for detecting danger)
one of the most extensively studied neural pathways serving this function is the so-called “low road” for emotion processing

steps.cellBodies: Sensory cortical association areas / primary sensory cortex
courseVia: thalamocortical pathway then corticoamygdala projection ("high road")
steps.terminatesIn: lateral nucleus and basolateral nuclei of the amygdala
steps.neurotransmitter: glutamate (not explicitly stated for this step)

evidence.quote: the canonical auditory thalamocortical pathway (MGB-primary auditory cortex; PAC; Table 2), used here as a proxy for the cortical “high road.”

courseVia: intra-amygdaloid excitatory glutamatergic pathway with relay through inhibitory GABAergic/intercalated interneurons

evidence.quote: The basolateral nuclei of amygdala collect sensory input from the cortical association area, prefrontal cortex, thalamus and hippocampus through lateral nucleus.

Basolateral nucleus processes this information and sends it to the central nucleus of amygdala through excitatory glutamatergic pathway along with relay of inhibitory GABAergic interneuron/intercalated neurons.
The main output pathway of amygdala is central nucleus.

steps.cellBodies: Central nucleus of the amygdala (GABAergic output neurons)
steps.terminatesIn: hypothalamus and brainstem (autonomic and somatic effector centres)

evidence.quote: Activation of inhibitory GABAergic neurons in the central nucleus leads to the development of autonomic and somatic signals of fear in the hypothalamus and brainstem.
Amygdala has neural circuits to carry out its different functions with two major output pathways; the Dorsal route via stria terminalis that projects to the septal area and hypothalamus

steps.terminatesIn: septal area, hypothalamus, and medial dorsal thalamic nucleus

evidence.quote: the ventral route via the ventral amygdalofugal pathway which terminates in the septal area, hypothalamus, and the medial dorsal thalamic nucleus

courseVia: projections to bed nucleus of the stria terminalis (BNST)
steps.terminatesIn: hypothalamus and brainstem structures (sustained anxiety response)

evidence.quote: BLA also activates the cells in the BNST to the hypothalamus and brainstem structures for autonomic & somatic signs of anxiety
Central nucleus pathway triggers short term & result in sensation of fear and bed nucleus of stria-terminalis pathway leads to long-term activation & general signs of anxiety

lesions.site: Bilateral amygdala / bilateral medial temporal lobe
lesions.deficit: Klüver-Bucy syndrome: hyperorality, hypersexuality, hyper-metamorphosis, placidity, bulimia, visual agnosia and amnesia

evidence.quote: Kluver-Bucy syndrome (KBS) is a rare neuropsychiatric condition caused by the abrasions which disturbs the hippocampus, bilateral temporal lobes of amygdala. The pathological characteristics are hyperorality, hypersexuality, hyper-metamorphosis, placidity, bulimia, visual agnosia and amnesia.

unsourced: The periaqueductal gray (PAG) and additional brainstem autonomic nuclei are classically described as downstream targets of the central nucleus of the amygdala for freezing and autonomic fear responses; no openable source explicitly naming the PAG in this exact amygdala-efferent context was found in this session.

The basolateral amygdala's fear-conditioning plasticity is generally attributed to glutamatergic (NMDA/AMPA receptor-dependent) synaptic transmission; not explicitly quoted with a citation for this batch.

pathways.name: Mesolimbic and mesocortical dopamine (reward) pathways, with nigrostriatal and tuberoinfundibular pathways for contrast
pathways.function: Reward, motivation and incentive salience (mesolimbic/mesocortical); motor control (nigrostriatal); neuroendocrine prolactin regulation (tuberoinfundibular)

evidence.quote: The mesolimbic pathway projects from the ventral tegmental area (VTA) to the ventral striatum.
The MFB is the most prominent mesolimbic reward pathway connecting the ventral tegmental areas with the prefrontal cortex
The MFB connects the midbrain's periaqueductal gray matter (PAG) to the ventral tegmental areas and the prefrontal cortex (PreFr).
The mesocortical pathway projecting from the VTA to the prefrontal cortex is, in turn, more involved in executive functions although it also contributes to reward processing.

steps.cellBodies: Substantia nigra pars compacta dopaminergic neurons

evidence.quote: The nigrostriatal pathway connects substantia nigra to the striatum (putamen and caudate) and contributes critically to motion control.

courseVia: tuberoinfundibular pathway to the median eminence / hypophyseal portal system

evidence.quote: Finally, the tuberoinfundibular pathway connects the hypothalamus and the pituitary gland.

unsourced: Degeneration of nigrostriatal dopaminergic neurons is the classic anatomical substrate of the motor deficits of Parkinson's disease; not explicitly quoted with a citation in the sources opened for this batch.
Tuberoinfundibular dopamine acts on pituitary lactotroph D2 receptors to tonically inhibit prolactin secretion; general endocrinology fact not directly quoted from an opened source in this session.

pathways.name: Ascending arousal system and the sleep-wake flip-flop switch
pathways.function: Maintenance of cortical arousal and wakefulness, and the reciprocal switching between wake- and sleep-promoting circuits

steps.cellBodies: Pedunculopontine (PPT) and laterodorsal tegmental (LDT) cholinergic nuclei (midbrain/pons)
courseVia: ascending cholinergic projection of the reticular activating system

evidence.quote: The lateral and dorsal pedunculopontine tegmentum contains primarily cholinergic neurons in neighboring groups within the midbrain and pons.
Cholinergic neurons project to the thalamus and cortex, promoting desynchronization of the brain,

steps.terminatesIn: cortex, thalamus, hypothalamus and basal forebrain

evidence.quote: The locus coeruleus is located within the upper dorsolateral pons of the brainstem. It is activated directly by orexin from the lateral hypothalamus, and in response, releases norepinephrine.
The raphe nuclei are located midline throughout the brainstem within the pons, midbrain, and medulla. The majority of neurons located in the raphe nuclei are serotonergic.

VLPO-related inhibitory output targets multiple wake-promoting nuclei—including the histaminergic tuberomammillary nucleus (TMN), noradrenergic locus coeruleus (LC), serotonergic raphe nuclei, and cholinergic neurons of the basal forebrain—thereby lowering cortical arousal and stabilizing sleep states
evidence.species: human (review synthesising rodent and human data)

steps.cellBodies: Orexin/hypocretin neurons of the lateral hypothalamus
steps.terminatesIn: locus coeruleus, tuberomammillary nucleus, raphe nuclei, basal forebrain and cortex

evidence.quote: these centers are activated by the lateral hypothalamus (LH), which releases the neuropeptide orexin in response to the light hitting the eyes, which then stimulates arousal and the transition from sleep to waking.

steps.cellBodies: Ventrolateral preoptic nucleus (VLPO), GABA/galanin co-expressing and non-galanin GABAergic neurons
steps.terminatesIn: tuberomammillary nucleus, locus coeruleus, raphe nuclei, basal forebrain and vlPAG/LDT-PPT (reciprocal inhibition of arousal nuclei)

evidence.quote: sleep–wake control has classically been conceptualized through the “flip-flop switch” model, in which sleep-promoting preoptic neurons and arousal-promoting systems engage in reciprocal inhibition to permit rapid and stable state transitions
evidence.species: human (review synthesising rodent and human data)

evidence.quote: including GABA/galanin co-expressing neurons, non-galanin GABAergic neurons, and glutamatergic neurons—contribute differentially to non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep, rapid eye movement (REM)-associated processes

steps.cellBodies: Ventrolateral periaqueductal gray (vlPAG) GABAergic REM-off neurons
courseVia: projections to pontine LDT/PPT cholinergic REM-promoting circuitry
steps.terminatesIn: laterodorsal tegmental (LDT) and pedunculopontine tegmental (PPT) nuclei
steps.neurotransmitter: GABA (vlPAG output); dopaminergic neurons also present in vlPAG per brief

evidence.quote: inhibition of vlPAG GABAergic REM-off neurons disinhibits pontine REM-promoting circuitry, thereby facilitating REM expression

lesions.site: Bilateral paramedian midbrain/pontine tegmentum and ascending reticular activating system
lesions.deficit: Coma: sustained unresponsiveness with eyes closed, unarousable to vigorous stimulation

evidence.quote: Acute impairments of consciousness include coma which is defined as a “state of unresponsiveness in which the patient lies with eyes closed and cannot be aroused to respond appropriately to stimuli even with vigorous stimulation”

unsourced: Dopaminergic neurons of the ventrolateral periaqueductal gray (vlPAG) are described in current sleep literature as an additional wake-promoting monoaminergic group; the vlPAG dopamine cell group's projections to hypothalamus/basal forebrain specifically were not found described with a quotable, openable source in this session.

pathways.name: Hypothalamo-pituitary axes (magnocellular neurohypophyseal and parvocellular adenohypophyseal / HPA axis)
pathways.function: Neuroendocrine control of water balance, lactation/uterine contraction (posterior pituitary) and anterior pituitary trophic hormone release, including the stress (HPA) axis

steps.cellBodies: Magnocellular neurons of the supraoptic nucleus (SON) and paraventricular nucleus (PVN)

evidence.quote: The paraventricular and supraoptic nuclei both produce the peptides oxytocin and ADH, which are released from neuronal axons into the capillaries of the posterior pituitary.
Magnocellular neurons in the paraventricular and supraoptic nuclei produce arginine vasopressin.

In humans, PVN neurons display a similar magnocellular/parvocellular organization, with magnocellular cells releasing OT and VP systemically and parvocellular cells regulating neuroendocrine and autonomic processes.

steps.cellBodies: Parvocellular neurosecretory neurons of the paraventricular nucleus (PVN)
courseVia: tuberoinfundibular tract to the median eminence, then hypophyseal portal system
steps.neurotransmitter: corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH), thyrotropin-releasing hormone, gonadotropin-releasing hormone

evidence.quote: PNCs synthesize hypophysiotropic hormones—including corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH), thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH), gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH), and somatostatin—and project to the median eminence, where they release these hormones into the hypophyseal portal system.
The arcuate nucleus releases hormones secreted by axon terminals into the hypothalamohypophysial venous portal system to control anterior pituitary hormone release.
Corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH), synthesized and secreted by the paraventricular nucleus of the hypothalamus, stimulates the anterior pituitary to release ACTH.
ACTH then acts on the adrenal cortex to promote cortisol synthesis and secretion.

steps.terminatesIn: hypothalamus and anterior pituitary (negative feedback) and peripheral target tissues

evidence.quote: This hormone functions as the primary glucocorticoid synthesized and released by the zona fasciculata of the adrenal cortex.
Cortisol exerts negative feedback on both the hypothalamus and anterior pituitary, inhibiting the secretion of CRH and ACTH, respectively.

conflicts.issue: Which adrenal cortical zone is stimulated by ACTH to produce cortisol

positions.claim: ACTH stimulates the zona fasciculata to produce the primary glucocorticoid cortisol
positions.quote: This hormone functions as the primary glucocorticoid synthesized and released by the zona fasciculata of the adrenal cortex.

positions.claim: ACTH stimulates the adrenal cortex zona reticularis to produce the stress-response hormone cortisol
positions.quote: ACTH travels through systemic circulation to stimulate the adrenal cortex (zona reticularis) production of the stress-response hormone cortisol.

unsourced: Non-neurosecretory parvocellular preautonomic neurons (PANs) of the PVN also send descending projections to autonomic centres in the brainstem and spinal cord (this pathway is more directly evidenced in the central autonomic control pathway entry of this batch).

pathways.name: Central autonomic control and micturition (hypothalamospinal, pontine micturition centre, Onuf's nucleus)
pathways.function: Descending hypothalamic control of spinal sympathetic outflow, and pontine coordination of bladder storage/voiding

steps.cellBodies: Hypothalamus (posterior/lateral hypothalamic neurons; first-order sympathetic neurons)
courseVia: descending hypothalamospinal tract, uncrossed through midbrain and pons
steps.terminatesIn: intermediolateral cell column (ciliospinal center of Budge, C8-T2)

evidence.quote: The first-order neurons originate in the hypothalamus and descend uncrossed through the midbrain and pons, terminating in the intermediolateral cell columns at the C8 through T2 levels of the spinal cord, known as the ciliospinal center of Budge.

courseVia: pelvic afferents to sacral cord, then spinoreticular/spinothalamic ascent to the periaqueductal gray (PAG)

evidence.quote: The central PAG receives afferents from the sacral cord, which in turn sends projections to the PMC.
When the urinary bladder becomes distended, the stretch receptors of the bladder wall transmits an afferent signal to the pons, which subsequent

courseVia: PAG-to-PMC projection (relay only, no direct PAG-to-sacral-motoneuron connection)

evidence.quote: PAG serves only as a relay station during transmission of afferents from the bladder to the PMC.
In fact, no direct connections exist between PAG and the sacral cord motoneurons.
The PMC, also known as Barrington's nucleus, is located in the brainstem and works with other regions of the brain to coordinate micturition.

It achieves this through activation of parasympathetic neurons, triggering the detrusor muscle to contract and indirectly inhibits the somatic nerves that maintain the external sphincter closed in contraction.
Pre-ganglionic parasympathetic nerve fibers exit the spinal cord primarily between S2 to S4.

courseVia: descending inhibitory pathway to Onuf's nucleus
steps.terminatesIn: Onuf's nucleus (sacral anterior horn) and external urethral sphincter (via pudendal nerve)
steps.neurotransmitter: acetylcholine (somatic pudendal output); inhibited during voiding

evidence.quote: External urethral sphincter relaxation is mediated indirectly by suppressing Onuf's nucleus located in the sacral spinal cord.

These neurons arise from Onuf's nucleus, located in the anterior horn of the sacral region of the spinal cord, and coalesce to become the pudendal nerve, which utilizes acetylcholine to contract the external urethral sphincter through stimulation of a nicotinic receptor at that site.

unsourced: The exact synaptic neurotransmitter used at hypothalamic (PVN/lateral hypothalamic) neurons projecting onto preganglionic sympathetic neurons of the intermediolateral column was not explicitly stated with a quotable citation in the sources opened this session.

Direct hypothalamic (PVN) projections specifically onto the sacral parasympathetic nucleus controlling the detrusor muscle (as distinct from the Barrington's-nucleus route) are described in classic neuroanatomy teaching but were not found with an openable, quotable source in this session.

Pontine stroke damaging Barrington's nucleus is classically associated with voiding dysfunction (e.g., Shukla R et al., BMJ Case Rep 2014, cited by S16) but the case report itself was not opened in full text this session, so this lesion claim is left unsourced rather than cited.

pathways.name: Circadian pathway: ipRGC to SCN to pineal melatonin
pathways.function: Photic entrainment of the master circadian clock and downstream control of pineal melatonin secretion

steps.cellBodies: Intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs), melanopsin-containing

decussation.where: a substantial component of the retinohypothalamic tract crosses in the optic chiasm to innervate both suprachiasmatic nuclei

steps.neurotransmitter: glutamate (retinal ganglion cell output; not explicitly stated for this exact step)

evidence.quote: Intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs) containing the blue light-sensitive photopigment melanopsin transmit light signals via the retinohypothalamic tract directly to the SCN, synchronizing SCN neurons to the external light-dark cycle.
During the daytime, light stimulates the retinohypothalamic pineal pathway. The retinal ganglion cells activate the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) through the optic nerve.

Specialized ganglia take the impulses generated by the light to the suprachiasmatic nucleus of the hypothalamus. The fibers from the hypothalamus then give off to the superior cervical ganglia in the spinal cord.

steps.terminatesIn: intermediolateral cell column of the upper thoracic spinal cord

evidence.quote: The first-order neurons originate in the hypothalamus and descend uncrossed through the midbrain and pons, terminating in the intermediolateral cell columns at the C8 through T2 levels of the spinal cord, known as the ciliospinal center of Budge.

steps.cellBodies: Intermediolateral cell column preganglionic sympathetic neurons
courseVia: preganglionic sympathetic fibres via the sympathetic chain

evidence.quote: Second-order preganglionic neurons exit the spinal cord at the T1 level and enter the cervical sympathetic chain, where they ascend to synapse in the superior cervical ganglion at the C3 through C4 levels.
From the spinal cord, signals are relayed back to the pineal gland via postganglionic neurons.
The sympathetic innervation is from the superior cervical ganglion, while the parasympathetic innervation is from the optic and pterygopalatine ganglia.

unsourced: At night, reduced SCN inhibition of the sympathetic pathway is generally described as disinhibiting norepinephrine release onto pinealocytes to drive melatonin synthesis; the specific mechanistic wording in the opened StatPearls chapter (S19) contained an apparent internal inconsistency (referring to melatonin release 'from the pituitary' in one sentence, though the chapter's own title and other sentences correctly identify the pineal gland as the source), so that specific sentence was not quoted verbatim for this fact.
Melatonin synthesis from serotonin via AANAT (arylalkylamine N-acetyltransferase) and HIOMT/ASMT enzymes was not found described with a quotable, openable source in this session.
